lines: * 🐛 `ObjectDominators.buildDominatorTree()` and `ObjectDominators.renderDominatorTree()` now compute the exact dominator tree with Lengauer-Tarjan instead of the approximation they used to share with the leak analysis, so the retained sizes they report are correct. On one of our test heap dumps, `class android.view.DisplayListCanvas` was reported as retaining 380748 bytes in 2600 objects when it actually retains 221 bytes in 4 objects.
* ⚠️ The `DominatorTree` class is gone, replaced by the new `shark.HeapDominatorTree`, which needs the whole graph up front.

* ⚠️ `ObjectDominators.DominatorNode.retainedSize` is a `Long` instead of an `Int`. It sums the shallow sizes of a whole subtree, so the root of the tree holds the size of the reachable heap and silently wrapped negative past 2 GB. That was reachable in alpha 9 too, but the exact tree is built for tools running on a workstation, where heap dumps that large are ordinary.

-* 🐛 A leak trace going through an entry of an object array reported the wrong index. The index was the position of that entry among the entries the analysis surfaces, which skip null entries and entries pointing to an object that isn't in the heap dump, rather than its position in the array, so each skipped entry ahead of it shifted the reported index down by one. The table of a hash based collection is mostly null entries, so a leak trace that goes through one — which is what LeakCanary reports when it doesn't recognize the collection and walks its internals instead of expanding it — said `[0]` whichever bucket the entry was really in. Leak signatures don't change: they already normalize every array index to `[x]`.

+* 🐛 A leak trace going through an entry of an object array reported the wrong index. The index was the position of that entry among the entries the analysis surfaces, which skip null entries and entries pointing to an object that isn't in the heap dump, rather than its position in the array, so each skipped entry ahead of it shifted the reported index down by one. The table of a hash based collection is mostly null entries, so a leak trace that goes through one — which is what LeakCanary reports when it doesn't recognize the collection and walks its internals instead of expanding it — said `[0]` whichever bucket the entry was really in. Leak fingerprints don't change: they already normalize every array index to `[x]`.

* 🐛 `ObjectDominators.buildDominatorTree()` and `ObjectDominators.renderDominatorTree()` only applied their `ignoredRefs` parameter when picking GC roots, and not when walking the heap. So they followed `WeakReference.referent`, `SoftReference.referent`, `PhantomReference.referent` and the finalizer list links no matter what was passed in, and reported memory as retained that garbage collection would reclaim. `ignoredRefs` now applies to the traversal too.

* 🐛 Heap growth detection computed the retained size of the objects it reports as growing from an approximate dominator tree built as the heap was traversed, an approximation that over attributes, sometimes by a lot. Retained sizes are now computed with the LeakShare metric from [BLeak](https://doi.org/10.1145/3192366.3192376), the paper heap growth detection is based on: the objects that are only reachable through the reported growing objects are credited to the growing objects that reach them.

* 🔀 An object that stays reachable without going through a growing object isn't counted anymore, and an object held by several growing objects is now split evenly between them instead of being counted in full for each, so the retained sizes reported change and are usually smaller. They add up to the size of the subgraph the growing objects hold together. The trade off is that the size reported for a single growing object isn't a lower bound of what fixing that one growing object would free, since freeing shared objects requires fixing every growing object that holds them.

* 🐛 `ServiceWatcher` stopped forwarding messages to a `Handler.Callback` already installed on `ActivityThread.mH` by something else, for every message whose `Message.obj` isn't an `IBinder` — which is most of them. That was collateral damage from the fix for [#2114](https://github.com/square/leakcanary/issues/2114), which returned early on those messages to avoid a `ClassCastException` on some Motorola ROMs.

* 🔀 `shark-cli dump-process` now asks the device to collect its garbage before writing the heap dump, with `am dumpheap -g`. Nothing else on that path collects: `am dumpheap` on its own writes whatever happens to be in the heap, and ART's hprof dumper suspends every thread rather than collecting, so a pulled dump held the live heap plus everything that had become garbage since the last collection. Measured on an API 29 emulator, dumping a real app's main process: 12.02 MB of the 92.9 MB of objects in the dump was unreachable, over 208733 objects, against 0.29 MB over 10467 objects for the same process dumped with `-g` a minute later. `-g` runs `System.gc()`, `System.runFinalization()` and `System.gc()` in the dumped process, the same trio LeakCanary runs before dumping its own heap, and it arrived in Android 8.1 — a device older than that is dumped without it, since it would refuse the whole command over an unknown option.

* 🔨 The LeakCanary task in Android Studio's Profiler keeps working on LeakCanary 3. Studio drives LeakCanary through a bridge library it injects into the app, [`com.android.tools.studio.leakcanary:leakcanary`](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/tools/base/+/refs/heads/mirror-goog-studio-main/studio-leakcanary/), which has no compile time dependency on LeakCanary and instead resolves every class, method and field it needs reflectively, by name, giving up on the whole integration at the first failed lookup — at which point Studio reports LeakCanary as missing from the app. All of those names survived LeakCanary 3 except the default `GcTrigger`, which used to be an object nested in `GcTrigger` and compiled to `leakcanary.GcTrigger$Default`, and is now `GcTrigger.inProcess()`. A class under the old name is published again for that lookup alone, deprecated so that no source reaches for it and documented as un-deletable. `AndroidStudioProfilerContractTest` replays the bridge's lookups against the `leakcanary-android` artifact, so the next rename fails there rather than silently in the IDE.

+* ⚠️ The hash that identifies a leak is now called its **leak fingerprint**: `LeakTrace.signature` and `Leak.signature` are `LeakTrace.leakFingerprint` and `Leak.leakFingerprint`, and `EventListener.Event.HeapAnalysisDone.HeapAnalysisSucceeded.unreadLeakSignatures` is `unreadLeakFingerprints`. The hash itself is unchanged — same input, same SHA-1 — so a leak keeps the string it already had, and a bug report or a dashboard grouped by it still lines up across the upgrade. The rename is about the word: *signature* is what a Kotlin or Java developer meeting it for the first time reads as a method signature, or as the signature an APK is signed with, and both of those also appear in LeakCanary's own code and change log. It also never said what the hash is *for*, which is that two leaks with the same one are caused by the same bug.

+    * 🔀 A heap analysis printed to Logcat or shared as text now reads `Leak fingerprint: <hash>` where it read `Signature: <hash>`, and *"Displaying only 1 leak trace out of N with the same leak fingerprint"* where it read *"…with the same signature"*. Anything parsing that text needs updating.
